newsitem.title: USA: Insured damage from Fran put at $625 million.
newsitem.headline: Insured damage from Fran put at $625 million.

text.p: Hurricane Fran delivered a destructive blow to the Carolina coast on Thursday, but the storm fell far short of turning into another Hurricane Hugo.
Although the work of sifting through the wreckage has just begun, a preliminary industry estimate of insured damage was put at about $625 million.
That would make it the seventh most costly hurricane, well behind Hurricanes Andrew and Hugo, the two most costly U.S. hurricanes on record.
Insured damage from Andrew in 1992 totalled about $15.5 billion and the damage from Hugo was about $4.2 billion, with $2.5 billion of that in the United States.
Fran, which at one point took aim at Charleston, S.C., rekindled memories of Hugo, which battered the city seven years ago.
But Fran's 115 mph (185 kmh) winds never quite matched the strength of Hugo's and the storm veered north of the stately city, making landfall in a less densely populated area of North Carolina.

"It's a major hurricane and a major loss, but it was not an Andrew and it was not a Hugo," said Sean Mooney, economist and senior vice president at the Insurance Information Institute, a trade group sponsored by the property-casualty insurance industry.
Applied Insurance Research in Boston prepared the preliminary estimate, using a computer software programme, the Insurance Information Institute said.
Risk Management Solutions in Menlo Park, Calif., said it estimated insured losses in a range from $300 million to $660 million, with its best estimate at $450 million.
Losses could still increase, however, as the industry assesses damage from inland areas, Mooney said.
But the losses will still be well within what the insurance industry expects to handle in a normal hurricane season.
The storm will not have a major impact on the financial strength of the insurance industry and the industry has the resources to pay the claims, he said.
"This is the type of storm we expect to get every two or three years," he said. "This level of losses is what we anticipate," he said.
"The general reaction is, it's unfortunate, but we're breathing a sigh of relief," he said.
However, overall catastrophic losses are running slightly ahead of average at about $5 billion so far this year and more losses are still possible as the hurricane season runs through November.

Blizzards and bitter cold resulted in insured losss of $2.55 billion in the first quarter of 1996. Severe thunderstorms, tornadoes and hail tacked on another $1.65 billion in insured losses in the second quarter.
That made the first half of 1996 the second costliest in the past 14 years.
Hurricane Bertha, which struck the eastern United States in early July, caused an estimated $194 million in insured losses.
"This has been a pretty tough year," said Jeff Thompson, an analyst with insurance research firm Conning & Co.
